references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C109 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ Daniel Cloak was wiping flour off his apron at a West Oakland bakery when he told Carmen Delaine what he thought of the Stabilization Fund. "It feels like something big, but I'm waiting to see it in action." That was the week in one sentence, and it wasn't only West Oakland talking. The fund has passed and money is moving, but as Carmen reported, the people it was built to keep in their homes are still watching. Irene Fay, who pulls morning shifts at a coffee shop nearby, says people are hopeful and skeptical at once. Darius Clark knows exactly what the fund is for and hasn't seen a change on his block. Elena Patel heard about it at the community center last month and still hasn't noticed anything. I don't read that as ingratitude. I read it as people who have watched promises travel slower than they sound.

THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C110 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ Three times this week, someone in Oakland told me something was moving, and three times I went looking for the motion. Start with West Oakland. Marcus Webb told the Finance Committee that seventy-nine households have been stabilized in nine months, and he put it the way a man does when the auditors are in the room: families with checks in hand before the notices arrive, every dollar moving through compliance. Carmen Delaine reported the fund's pace, a little over three weeks from application to money. Mayor Santana called it "relief without bureaucracy." Those two ideas sit uncomfortably together. A fund that is proud of how well it passes scrutiny is not a fund without bureaucracy. It may be a good bureaucracy, and I'd rather have a careful one than a reckless one, but let's not pretend it's something else.

Now set that beside what Jordan Velez found a few blocks over. Oakmesh, Civis Systems and Coastline Construction are all growing along the same West Oakland lane, and the money there is not waiting for anyone. Enzo Walker, a plumber at Oakmesh, told Jordan he spends half his days fixing pipes in buildings that didn't exist last year. "The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here." His colleague Dom Will sees the same growth and calls it something real, not a bubble. Sam Fazio at Civis calls it a shared project. Maybe it is. But a neighborhood can have a crane on every corner and a fund in its disbursement phase and still be asking where the help is. Enzo has the quote of the week: "We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us." Private money arrived fast and visible this week. Public money meant to hold people in place has not yet shown itself. I'd like someone to tell me which of those is outrunning the other.

============================================================ By Jordan Velez | Bay Tribune Business West Oakland’s new business money is moving faster than the block can absorb Enzo Walker spends his working days at Oakmesh Systems keeping water moving through buildings that, in his telling, keep appearing around him. He is a plumber at the West Oakland civic-tech company, working alongside Elijah Roberts, Dom Will and Jace Robinson. Oakmesh, Civis Systems and Coastline Construction are all expanding along the same West Oakland business lane. Those are strong signs. They are also not the same thing as money settling into the neighborhood.

“Honestly? Those tech firms like Oakmesh and Civis—they're changing the block faster than we can keep up. I work at Oakmesh, and half the time I'm fixing pipes in buildings that didn't exist last year. The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here. Guys like Elias at Civis talk about 'systems' and 'efficiency,' but ask the folks at the bus stop if they feel any of that. We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us.” Walker said. The contrast is visible in the roster itself. Oakmesh’s named jobs range from construction labor and plumbing to machine learning. Civis lists Sam Fazio and Catherine Santos as digital twin architects, Elias Varek as founder and Maurice Franklin as drone fleet coordinator. Coastline’s managing partner is Desmond Achebe. Mariner Construction and Northgate Construction are also part of the construction economy around the lane.

============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic Nine Months, Seventy-Nine Households: The Stabilization Fund Moves at a 23-Day Pace By Carmen Delaine Marcus Webb sat in the Finance Committee chamber with a single line of data that carried the weight of displacement pressure: seventy-nine households stabilized in nine months. He framed the number not as a victory lap but as evidence of traction. "Seventy-nine households stabilized means seventy-nine Oakland families with checks in hand before the displacement notices arrive," Webb said, his tone calibrated to the auditors tracking compliance. Every dollar, he added, moves with the compliance that passes the Finance Committee's scrutiny.

The West Oakland Stabilization Fund, proposed by Mayor Avery Santana and signed into law in Cycle 78 with a 6-3 council vote, is now moving checks through the real machinery of bureaucracy. Cycle 110 marked the ninth month of active disbursement, and the Initiative_Tracker logs the arc: $400,000 approved for Month-Nine, with a 23-day average processing window achieved. The fund's total envelope was $28 million. It has disbursed, in visible tranche, $81,188 in household grants by the end of Cycle 109, and now carries $23 million remaining.

The name of the game, as framed by the officials steering it, is speed wrapped in compliance. That friction—moving cash without creating audit liability—is where the story sits this cycle. Denise Carter, City Council District 1, had already staked her position earlier in the cycle on where that friction resolves. "When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving," she said. The language was deliberate: the fund is not a static account waiting for applications; it is a tool meant to track and intercept displacement as it moves. The implication was that West Oakland's commercial core and its residential stability are yoked.

Mayor Santana pressed the speed narrative. "Nine months in, we're proving that relief without bureaucracy keeps neighbors in their neighborhoods," she said in her cycle-110 office record. The claim nested two things: that the mechanism was working, and that other cities or prior efforts had let bureaucracy be the obstacle. Brenda Okoro, in her own statement, refined it further. "Nine months in, the Fund's design is holding—targeted relief that flows to tenants before displacement does," she said. The sequence matters—relief first, displacement second, not the other way around.

============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic West Oakland Stabilization Fund Enters Ground Phase—But the Money's Visibility Remains Unclear Daniel Cloak stood behind the counter at the bakery in West Oakland, wiping flour dust from his apron. The morning rush had cleared, and he leaned against the register with the kind of patient skepticism that comes from living in a neighborhood long enough to watch promises move slower than they sound. "I've heard folks talking about the Stabilization Fund at the bakery, but honestly, I'm not sure yet how it's touching the ground here," he said. "It feels like something big, but I'm waiting to see it in action."

That wait—the gap between a fund's official disbursement phase and the moment residents feel its weight on their block—is the ledger's current problem. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund entered its disbursement-active phase this cycle. The Initiative passed. The money is moving through the city's machinery. Yet four weeks into implementation, the people it was built to hold in place remain in the posture of watching. Irene Fay, a barista working the morning shift at a West Oakland coffee shop, had heard the same conversations Cloak tracked at his counter. "I've heard folks at the coffee shop talking about the Stabilization Fund, but honestly, it's hard to tell where that money's actually going. People seem hopeful but also kinda skeptical—like they're waiting to see if it'll really make a difference on our block."

The skepticism is not misplaced. Initiative_Tracker records show the fund's status as passed and active in disbursement phase as of this cycle. That designation means the decision is made and the allocation mechanism is live. It does not yet mean the money has landed in the hands of the people it aims to stabilize—the renters, the long-term residents, the households that have held ground in West Oakland as the city has shifted around them. The fund was designed to keep people in their homes. Darius Clark, another bakery regular in the neighborhood, had absorbed the purpose. "I heard about that fund at the bakery—couple regulars were talking how it's supposed to help keep folks in their homes. Haven't seen much change on my block yet, but I hope it works out."

Elena Patel, a resident, echoed the gap between announcement and arrival. "I heard about the Stabilization Fund at the community center last month, but honestly, I haven't noticed any changes on my block yet." The civic record identifies the Initiative as active in disbursement. The people living under its intended reach report a wait. Neither observation is false. The fund is moving; the ground has not yet shifted. This is the moment where implementation clocks and lived time diverge—where a ledger entry says "phase disbursement-active" and a neighborhood watches for proof.

Dom Will, a machine learning engineer at Oakmesh, sees the same expansion from inside the company but reads its purpose differently. “Oakmesh feels like we're building something real here - not just another tech bubble. Marcus keeps us focused on civic impact, not just profit. Civis down the street? Elias runs a tight ship, all that urban intelligence work. You see their drone fleet buzzing around sometimes. Coastline's got cranes up everywhere - hard to miss them. But it's the small crews, like our construction guys, that make the neighborhood hum.”

There is also a gap in the arithmetic nobody has explained. The fund was sized at $28 million. Carmen's reporting has about $81,000 in household grants out the door by the end of last cycle, and the same reporting puts the remainder at $23 million. Those figures don't reconcile. Maybe the difference is money committed but not yet paid, or money in another category. Maybe it's a reporting slip. Webb and the Finance Committee can tell us which. Denise Carter said it plainly, "When storefronts go quiet, families go next," and if that's the thesis, residents deserve a clear answer on how much of the money is actually reaching them.

The question for the city offices managing this fund is not whether it was passed. It is whether the velocity between approval and ground-level arrival can close before the residents watching for it lose faith that it will arrive at all. The next scheduled action is Month-Ten disbursement review in Cycle 111. That checkpoint will show whether the 23-day window holds, whether the pace of cash flow accelerates or stalls, and whether the remaining $23 million carries the same gravity in the tenth month as it did in the ninth. The extraction question Webb's own language raised but could not answer: Are seventy-nine households enough to hold the line in West Oakland's commercial districts before the next wave of displacement notices arrive?

Luis was fair about it. He didn't call anyone a liar. He said what he doesn't have: when the listening sessions happened, who sat in them, which office owns the next step. I'd add only this. The riders are arriving in Fruitvale now. The merchants have been promised they'll be heard. The people designing the future of that corridor have said the same sentence for three cycles, and a sentence repeated is not progress made. Then there's the Oaks, where the opposite problem is playing out. Nobody is overpromising. Everyone is hoping. Talia Finch found Jessie Hess in a Dimond bar, holding her drink in both hands, wanting to believe and unable to. The expansion club finished preseason 0-5, and by Talia's count 0-9 once rookie camp is included. P Slayer caught Hess outside the arena, shoulders tight, saying she was hyped about the starting five and then watched the Heat game. P Slayer called the exits-before-the-buzzer scene "the sound of the same story starting again." That's the sharper take. Talia's is the more generous one, and I think it's the truer read: Daniel Cloak says the Oaks are genuinely reaching out to the community and that counts for something. Melton Neilon, who bakes sourdough, says the Oaks aren't what keeps him up at night. His regulars are. I wouldn't wave that off. A club can't ask people to care before it has given them a night worth retelling, and a baker's regulars have already gotten theirs.

“Honestly, I'm still trying to process how the Oaks did in their preseason games,” Hess says. “I was really looking forward to seeing what they could do, but that loss to the Miami Heat was a letdown. I want to believe they can turn it around, but it's hard to shake off the feeling that it's going to be a tough season.” The final preseason loss left the Oaks at 0-5 in preseason and winless at 0-9 through rookie camp and preseason. The room mood is frustrated, and the fan read is low. Those numbers sit on the screen like a tab nobody wants to pick up.

Daniel Cloak was there too, wiping flour off his hands from the late shift at the bakery, nodding like he’d heard the same line from half the line that came through his counter. “I still feel that way about the Oaks, they’re trying to reach out and be part of the community, and that’s something positive. Even with the preseason loss to the Miami Heat, I believe their effort to connect with us is genuine and that’s what matters to me.” We walked a block toward the BART stop with the 0-5 record sitting on us like wet concrete. Five straight losses before the real games even start. That number doesn’t lie. Some fans will tell you preseason is just noise, that the streak means nothing once opening night hits. They’re wrong. A winless run this long already tells you the habits that are baked in, the same ones that let a team walk off the floor flat after another loss to Miami. We felt it in the stands—empty applause, the slow drift toward the exits before the buzzer. That isn’t noise. That’s the sound of the same story starting again.

The final preseason game made the same point in a different arrangement. Adash Stanley finished with eight points and 11 assists. Dybantsa had 11 points. The feed also recorded a 20-point line for Austin Reaves. The Oaks lost again, this time to finish 0-5 and winless as a franchise between rookie camp and preseason. The useful question is therefore not whether the Oaks have players capable of producing numbers. The record already answers that. The question is whether those numbers connect across games. Stanley’s 11 assists point to distribution; Reaves’ scoring lines point to a primary offensive role; Dybantsa’s 22-point and 11-point games show a young scorer whose output moved from one result to the next. None of those facts, by themselves, explains how the lineup is supposed to hold together.

============================================================ By Selena Grant | Bay Tribune Sports The Oaks’ First Board Read Is a Blank One Selena Grant | Bay Tribune Sports Austin Reaves finished with 17 points and five assists, while AJ Dybantsa had 22 points and six rebounds. The Oaks still lost their fourth straight preseason game, leaving the expansion franchise at 0-4. That result established the first problem with reading this roster through individual production alone. The scoring lines are present. The record is not. Reaves supplied a creation line, and Dybantsa supplied the larger scoring total, but the Oaks’ board still showed another loss. For a first-year club, that distinction matters: a promising player line can describe development without yet describing a functioning team.

Wilson Shepard has reassured that the full team has yet to suit up as one. That leaves the Oaks with an opening, but not yet an attachment. Can the first games turn effort into a reason to come back? The screen keeps glowing above the bar. Hess lowers her drink. Nobody cheers. Nobody leaves. That is the expansion-board read from Dimond: the club has individual evidence, but no winning evidence yet. The five-game record does not prove that the roster cannot work. It does establish that the current build has not converted its best statistical lines into a result. The franchise’s stability remains uncertain because the record offers no settled answer about which production is foundational and which is situational. The matchup against the club where Paulson ran the front office last season adds an unavoidable layer to the ledger. The Oaks lost that game, too. The significance is not that one opponent can define an expansion team; it is that the loss leaves the organization with no preseason result to counter the cold start.

Selena Grant's board read gets at the practical problem. Austin Reaves, AJ Dybantsa and Adash Stanley all put up lines, and Stanley had eleven assists in the finale. The lines are fine, and the record is zero wins. Her point is that the front office owes the public a decision about which production is foundational and which is situational. I'll go further: that decision is the whole job. One small thing for the record: the feed carried both a 17-point and a 20-point line for Reaves in different games, and I'd like someone to confirm which belongs where before we build anything on it.

A turnaround begins with a decision the front office still owes the record: which number is the starting point for the build? Is it Stanley’s distribution, Reaves’ scoring, Dybantsa’s ceiling, or a structure that has not yet appeared in the results? Until the answer produces something beyond another individual line, the Oaks remain 0-5, and the key to the turnaround is still an open question. ============================================================ By P Slayer | Bay Tribune Sports I caught up with Jessie Hess on the sidewalk outside the arena after the final horn, her shoulders still tight from sitting through the whole thing. She didn’t need long to say what the rest of us were chewing on. “Honestly, I’m a bit disappointed after their last preseason game. I was really hyped about the Oaks’ starting five and their chances this season, but losing to the Miami Heat doesn’t exactly fill me with confidence. I still want to believe they can turn it around, though.”

The question in Dimond is not only whether the Oaks can win. It is whether a club can ask people to care before it has given them a night they want to retell. Daniel Cloak keeps the door open. “I still feel that way about the Oaks, they're really making an effort to be part of the community and that's something positive. I've seen it with the preseason games, they're trying to reach out and it's great to see.” That is the second story in the room, quieter than the losses: an effort can be visible and still not be enough to make a fan. The Oaks are trying to reach the neighborhood while the neighborhood is trying to work out what, exactly, it is being reached for.

Melton Neilon has a different measure. “Honestly, I still don't really know what to make of the Oaks analysis. As a sourdough baker, I'm more focused on getting my bread just right than following sports news. I've got my regulars to think about and making sure they've got their favorite loaves. That's what keeps me up at night, not the Oaks' preseason games.” Rick Walker has heard the talk but has not found a clean answer in it. “Honestly, I'm still trying to keep up with the news like everyone else, but it's tough when the team's performance is all over the place. I've heard some folks talking about Oaks analysis around the neighborhood, seems like people are trying to make sense of what's going on with the team.”

The fog and gray were all over the week, by the way. Noah Tan's pieces have Colin Soria blowing on his hands outside the laundromat, and the people he talked to called the weather "neutral" and "deliberate." I'll take the dull gray days as a small mercy. They gave the city a week to slow down and notice things. On the field, Simon Leary wrote the most careful column of the week about the A's. They are 1-0 and have won two straight, and there's a role change on the team that nobody has explained. I can't square 1-0 with two straight wins either, and I won't pretend to. Simon's restraint is right. A record is a beam, not a forecast. And over in Rockridge, Nia Rook found the neighborhood still lit up after Otis Redd's night on UNDOCKED, a 143-credit swing that has people arguing about who holds the edge and for how long. Rockridge, sitting at the top of the school table, can afford the entertainment. I won't begrudge anyone a good night.

What does the role change reveal about the A’s approach to maintaining their current record? At 1-0, with 2 straight wins, the record can show that the structure is standing. It cannot yet say who built it, why it was altered, or how long it will bear the weight.
